newsitem.title: USA: Flooded Ohio River hits transport fuel shipments.
newsitem.headline: Flooded Ohio River hits transport fuel shipments.

text.p: Flooding on the Ohio River is forcing delays in oil product shipments to a number of major oil company terminals, disrupting the distributon of gasoline and other transportation fuels in the region.

Ashland Inc's Catlettsburg, Kentucky refinery and terminals run by British Petroleum, Exxon Corp, Shell Oil Co and Chevron Corp were the largest of the companies suffering delays, a Coast Guard offical said Thursday.

Coast Guard officials stopped shipping on the Ohio River in the early morning hours on Monday. Barge traffic may resume in a few days, as long as no damage from floating debris is detected, one Coast Guard official said.

The Ashland Catlettsburg refinery, with a capacity of 219,000 barrels per day, shut three "supplemental" units as a precautionary measure, said Ashland spokesman Chuck Rice, but that the plant has not run below capacity.
"Operations are returning to normal," Rice added.
Ashland moved two barges of gasoline out of storage at Catlettsburg early this week before those tanks could be threatened by flood waters, according to the Coast Guard.

BP was "experiencing some difficulty" in product movements at its terminals, said company spokeswoman Linda McRae. All terminals were open, though the company provided no details on the movement of specific cargoes.

With flood waters running over locks and dams on the Ohio River, areas downstream of the Catlettsburg refinery are experiencing loading delays, and five or six tanks at the company's Cincinnati terminal that are under water.
Some 711,000 barrels of product are stored in 31 tanks at the Cincinnati facility, Rice said. That terminal is flooded on both the river and road sides, which prevents movement of product by truck.
Storms ravaged the region from Arkansas to West Virginia, raising the Ohio River to its highest crest in three decades and killing at least 57 people.
The Ohio River actually dropped a few inches Thursday morning from its crest at 64.7 feet late Wednesday, which is about 12 feet above flood stage.
The flooding forced about 30 oil and chemical terminals in region to delay loadings, according to Coast Guard officials in Huntington, West Virginia.
-- Matt Daily, New York Energy Desk + 1 212 859 1620
